explanations.answer: The one whose transgressions are forgiven
explanations.explanation: David says, "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven…" The blessing goes to the forgiven one. That's good news for anybody who has ever scorched a whole tray and had to face the family. I'd take forgiven over flawless any day, friend.

explanations.answer: The one who has never sinned at all
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say that. He says, "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered." The blessed one is the forgiven one, not someone with a spotless record. If a spotless record were the requirement, I'd be hanging my apron up right now.

explanations.answer: The one who keeps every command
explanations.explanation: That's not what David sings here, friend. His opening line is, "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered." He puts the blessing on forgiveness, and he says nothing about a perfect score. I'd say that's a lot more comforting than a checklist.

Yes, friend. David says, "Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him, in whose spirit there is no deceit." So the blessed man is the forgiven one, and there's no deceit in his spirit. I think that sets up everything David says next.

It's True, friend. David says the blessed man is the one "…whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him, in whose spirit there is no deceit." Both halves are right there in verse 2. Easy to skim past, and I've skimmed past a recipe line or two myself.

That's it. David says, "When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long." The silence didn't bring him peace. It came with groaning, and all day long at that. I think anybody who has carried something around and refused to say it out loud knows that ache.

explanations.answer: He rested easy all day long
explanations.explanation: Not even close, friend. David says, "When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long." There was groaning all day, and no easy rest. That's the opposite of a nice nap by the oven.

I wish, friend, because I'd be first in line for a laughing day. But David says, "When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long." The all-day part was groaning. Later the psalm does call for rejoicing.

It's False, friend. David tells the LORD, "For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat." His strength was drained, and it did not hold up just fine. Drained is about as far from "just fine" as you can get.

Right, it's False. David says, "For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat." Drained is about as far from "just fine" as you can get. I think this part of the psalm is heavy, so let's give it room.

Yes, hide. David says, "Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity." The silence is over. He stops keeping it under wraps and brings it out to the LORD. Friend, that's the turn in the whole psalm.

Close in spirit, friend, but it flips the verse. David did admit it. The verse says, "…I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity." So "not admit" would mean the exact opposite of what he did. One little word, and the whole batch changes.

The verse doesn't use that word. David says, "Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity." The word that fits is hide, because he stopped hiding it. Regret never comes up in this line.

explanations.answer: He forgives the guilt of his sin
explanations.explanation: That's it. David says, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD…" and then he tells Him, "…You forgave the guilt of my sin." Friend, look at the order. He confesses, and forgiveness is right there. After all that groaning, I think that's the best line in the psalm.

explanations.answer: He lays a penalty on him
explanations.explanation: That's not what David tells us. He says, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD…" and "…You forgave the guilt of my sin." The word is forgave, not penalty. I'd be waiting by the oven for a bill that never comes.

explanations.answer: He turns His face from him
explanations.explanation: Nothing like that here, friend. After David says, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD…" he tells God, "…You forgave the guilt of my sin." The psalm shows forgiveness, not a turned face. Same door he came in through, wide open.

explanations.answer: Pray to the LORD while He may be found
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David says, "Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found." He's turning his own story into an invitation for everyone godly. Pray, and don't put it off.

explanations.answer: Wait on the LORD until the storm has passed
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not David's line. He says, "Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found." The call is to pray, and he doesn't tell them to sit and wait it out. Bakers who stand around watching the oven timer know the difference.

explanations.answer: Keep silent before the LORD in their trouble
explanations.explanation: That one's backwards, friend. Silence is what David did back in verse 3, and it left him groaning. Now he says, "Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found." He learned that lesson the hard way, and he's passing it on.
That's right. David says, "Surely when great waters rise, they will not come near." Great waters can rise, and still they will not come near. I'd say that's a mighty comforting picture, friend.

It's True, friend. David says, "Surely when great waters rise, they will not come near." He does picture the waters rising, and he says they won't come near. This verse is more comforting than a warm cookie on a cold day.
Yes, deliverance. David tells the LORD, "You protect me from trouble; You surround me with songs of deliverance." I picture a whole choir around him, friend. Not a bad crowd to have in your corner.
Not this time, friend. David says, "You surround me with songs of deliverance." Mourning isn't what surrounds him here. He's got a whole round of songs about being rescued.
Songs of warning would just be a choir of smoke alarms, friend. Nobody wants that around them. David says, "You surround me with songs of deliverance." These songs are about being rescued.

That's it. David says, "Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding; they must be controlled with bit and bridle to make them come to you." Right after the line, "I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go…" this is the warning (Psalm 32:8). I think it's an invitation to listen and follow close.
The verse doesn't say that, friend. David says, "Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding…" It's understanding that's missing here. I wouldn't tell a horse he's weak, anyway.

Good guess, since a stubborn mule does seem short on patience. But David says, "Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding…" The word is understanding. Patience never shows up in the verse.
It's False, friend. David says, "Many are the sorrows of the wicked…" Many sorrows, and not just a few. Then he turns to the one who trusts in the LORD.

Right, it's False. The psalm says, "Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD." The wicked have many sorrows, and the verse sets that against the one who trusts. Two paths, side by side.
That's right. The psalm says, "…loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD." Surrounds, friend, like it's packed in all the way around. Like a cookie box with no empty corners.
That's not in the verse, friend. The psalm says, "…loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD." What surrounds the one who trusts is loving devotion. I'd take that over worry any day.
Nope, nobody's lurking in this verse. The psalm says, "…loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD." The thing that surrounds him is loving devotion. A much friendlier crowd.

explanations.answer: Be glad and shout for joy
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David ends with, "Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones; shout for joy, all you upright in heart." The man who groaned all day long now calls everyone to shout for joy. Go ahead, friend, and make some noise.

Not at the end of this psalm, friend. David closes with, "Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones; shout for joy, all you upright in heart." The call is to be glad and to shout for joy. Sorrow doesn't get the last word here.

David says the opposite, friend. He closes with, "Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones; shout for joy, all you upright in heart." Shout for joy is not a hidden thing. Earlier in the psalm David says, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD…" and he did not hide his iniquity (Psalm 32:5).
